newsitem.title: USA: Euro optimism steals the show at IMF talks.
newsitem.headline: Euro optimism steals the show at IMF talks.

text.p: European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Sunday an increasing number of countries may qualify for monetary union in 1999 after a series of tough budgets presented this month.

"I think a significant number will be ready in 1997. When I see the present efforts, I am optimistic," de Silguy told reporters during the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
"I think the number will be more on the increasing trend than the decreasing trend," he said.

The Commission had earlier suggested some seven European Union countries would meet Maastricht treaty standards in 1997, the key year for deciding which countries qualify to join a single currency in 1999.
But de Silguy declined to comment on whether Spain or Italy, which unveiled tough spending-cutting budgets last week, would make it into monetary union at the start, saying it was too early to judge.
Germany has long favoured starting Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) with some seven or so richer northern European states, to ensure the new euro becomes as stable a currency as the mark now is.

Officials said the question of the stability of the new euro had stolen much of the limelight both at the IMF talks, and at a meeting of finance ministers from the Group of Seven rich industrialized nations on Saturday.

"The others are interested in the fact that when the mark disappears, its successor currency should be able to take exactly the role of the mark," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference.
"Otherwise there could be flight into the dollar which would have consequences in the currency markets. No one is interested in that happening," he said.
Officials said the consensus that was emerging between finance ministers was that there would be a strong and stable euro, counterbalancing a strong dollar.

All G7 ministers agreed on Saturday that they backed a strong dollar, while European ministers stressed that their determination to maintain fiscal stability after the launch of the euro would underpin the fledgling currency.
"The euro will be as strong and as stable as the strongest currency in Europe," de Silguy said.
Helping the drive to EMU will be a pick-up in growth next year, forecast by the Commission to reach two to 2.5 percent on average in the European Union.
"Economic activity seems likely to be stronger in 1997... in Europe," IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said. "This will help the process toward monetary unification."
But officials warned that unemployment remained a blackspot in Europe.

"High rates of unemployment continue to trouble many nations in Europe, highlighting the importance of structural reforms that will enhance job creation and labour market flexibility," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said.
